notes.meaning: God told the Israelites that every seven years they had to cancel or release debts. This special year of rest gave poor borrowers a fresh start. It kept families from being trapped in permanent debt.

During this seventh year, no lender was allowed to demand repayment from a fellow Israelite. The Lord declared this time as His own season of release. Creditors were expected to reflect God's mercy by letting the debt go.

An Israelite could still collect money from a foreign merchant, but had to release what a fellow Israelite owed. Foreign travelers did not observe the land's rest year and continued to earn their usual income. The law protected members of the covenant family who had fallen on hard times.

God declared that there should be no poor among His people because He planned to bless them abundantly in the land. The laws on debt were designed to prevent poverty from taking root. When people cared for one another, no one would be left destitute.

This widespread blessing depended on the nation listening to God and obeying all His commands. God's promise of plenty went hand in hand with living out His covenant rules. Faithfulness to God was the key to their national prosperity.

When the Lord blessed Israel as He promised, they would become wealthy enough to lend money to other nations without needing to borrow. Their financial strength would give them independence and honor among their neighbors. Having plenty was a gift from God to be used wisely.

If a fellow Israelite became poor in any town, the people were forbidden to harden their hearts or close their fists. God commanded them to pay attention to needy neighbors right in their own communities. Selfishness toward a struggling brother was treated as a direct rebellion against God.

Instead of turning away, God's people were told to open their hands wide and lend whatever the poor person needed. Help was to be measured by the person's real need and the lender's ability to give. An open hand showed that the person's heart was truly tender toward God and others.

God warned against holding back a loan just because the seventh year was close at hand. A lender might worry that the debt would be cancelled before it could be repaid, but God called that kind of thinking wicked. If the poor person cried out to God in distress, the tightfisted lender was guilty of sin.

The people were told to give generously and with a willing, happy heart. God promised that cheerful generosity would bring His blessing on all their farming and daily work. Trusting God with money always leads to deeper blessing.

In a broken world, there will always be people who fall into poverty. Because need never disappears, God commands His people to keep their hands open to the poor at all times. Needy neighbors give God's people constant chances to show love in action.

If an Israelite man or woman had to sell themselves into service to pay off debts, they could only be held for six years. When the seventh year arrived, the owner was required to set them completely free. Servitude among God's people was never meant to be permanent.

When masters released their servants, they were strictly forbidden from sending them away empty-handed. Walking away with nothing would only force the freed servant back into debt and slavery. True freedom required real support.

Masters had to supply the freed servant generously with animals from the flock, grain from the threshing floor, and wine from the press. They were to give out of the abundance that God had given them. This gave the servant the basic tools needed to build a fresh, independent life.

Moses reminded Israel that they had once been enslaved in Egypt until the Lord redeemed them, buying back their freedom. Because God had shown them great mercy and brought them out with wealth, they were expected to treat their own workers with the same grace. Gratitude to God should always shape how we treat others.

Sometimes a servant loved the master and the household and was well cared for there. In that situation, the worker might choose to stay rather than take personal freedom. True loyalty and mutual respect made the master's home a place of safety and peace.

If a servant decided to stay, the master took an awl and pierced the servant's ear against the doorpost of the home. This visible mark showed everyone that the servant had willingly joined that family for life. Female servants who chose to remain were given the exact same honor and security.

Owners were told not to feel resentful when setting a servant free. Six years of faithful work had provided double the value of a regular hired worker who only worked day shifts for wages. God promised to reward and bless the master who obeyed this command without bitterness.

Every firstborn male animal from the cattle and sheep belonged to the Lord and had to be dedicated to Him. Owners were not allowed to put a firstborn bull to work in the field or shear the wool of a firstborn sheep. These animals were kept sacred because they reminded Israel of how God spared their own firstborn sons in Egypt.

Each year, the owner and his household were to bring these firstborn animals to the central place of worship chosen by God. There they enjoyed a sacred family feast in the presence of the Lord. Honoring God with the first and best of their herds became a time of shared joy and thanksgiving.

If a firstborn animal had a serious defect, such as being blind or lame, it could not be offered as a sacrifice to God. God will only accept what is whole and unblemished. Giving God an animal that was damaged or unwanted was no real sacrifice at all.

Even though a flawed firstborn could not be sacrificed at the sanctuary, the family could still butcher and eat it at home. In their hometowns, both ceremonially clean and unclean people were welcome to share the meat, just as they would eat wild game like deer. God provided food for His people even when an animal could not serve on the altar.

The only restriction was that the people were never allowed to eat the animal's blood. They had to drain it and pour it out on the ground like water. In God's law, blood represented the sacred gift of life, which belongs exclusively to the Creator.
